summary: Defines three Elliptic Curve Cryptography groups based on modular arithmetic modulo a prime, for use in IKE and IKEv2. They align the protocols with NIST standards and can be more efficient than earlier ECC groups. It is informational and replaced RFC 4753.

eli5.summary: Secret-sharing in IPsec uses special math shapes. This adds three more efficient shapes that match what other security systems already use.

subtitle: Three elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman groups for IKE and IKEv2, plus a corrected shared-secret format.

tldr.problem: IKE and IKEv2 needed more elliptic curve options that use ordinary prime-field arithmetic and line up with NIST and other standards, and RFC 4753 had left the shared-secret format ambiguous.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three random ECP groups (256, 384 and 521 bits), sets the format of the public values in the KE payload, and says the shared secret is the x value of the common point.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 4753 and fixes the shared-secret format that an erratum to RFC 4753 had already described.

facts.label: Shared secret
facts.value: x value of the common value

today: RFC 5903 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 4753. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Add More Groups
sections.content:
IKE and IKEv2 use a Diffie-Hellman exchange to create a shared secret. RFC 2409 defined five standard Oakley Groups: three modular exponentiation groups and two elliptic curve groups over GF[2^N]. Nineteen more were later assigned by IANA, and all of those are optional.

This RFC adds three ECP groups, which are elliptic curve groups modulo a prime. The RFC gives three reasons. The arithmetic is plain integer arithmetic modulo a prime rather than binary field arithmetic, so software can be more efficient. The groups are among those standardized by NIST, SECG, ISO and ANSI. And they can give security consistent with AES.
sections.eli5: Think of a menu of secret-handshake styles. This RFC adds three new styles that are quicker to do and that other systems already know.

sections.title: The Three ECP Groups
sections.content:
Implementations of IKE and IKEv2 SHOULD support each of the three groups. All use the curve equation y^2 = x^3 - 3x + b over the integers modulo a prime p.

  • 256-bit group: p = 2^256 - 2^224 + 2^192 + 2^96 - 1.
  • 384-bit group: p = 2^384 - 2^128 - 2^96 + 2^32 - 1.
  • 521-bit group: p = 2^521 - 1.

For each group the RFC lists the field size, the prime, the curve constant b, the group order and the generator point g = (gx, gy) in hexadecimal. Each group was chosen verifiably at random using SHA-1 as specified in IEEE 1363, from a published seed.
sections.eli5: Each group is a different-sized playground with its own fixed rules and starting spot. Bigger playgrounds are harder to cheat in.

sections.title: Key Exchange Data Formats
sections.content:
In an ECP key exchange, the Diffie-Hellman public value carried in a KE payload has two parts, x and y, the coordinates of a curve point. Each part MUST have a fixed bit length: 256 for the 256-bit group, 384 for the 384-bit group and 528 for the 521-bit group. Values are padded with leading zeros when needed. The public value is the x and y values concatenated.

The shared secret is the x value of the Diffie-Hellman common value. The RFC says these formats are specific to ECP curves and may not apply to EC2N curves.
sections.eli5: Each public number is written on a form with a fixed number of boxes, and unused boxes are filled with zeros. The final secret is just one of the two numbers from the answer.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4753
sections.content:
RFC 4753 said the shared secret had the same format as the public value. This RFC replaces that with the rule that the shared secret is the x value of the common value, which aligns the format with other standards. The change had already appeared as an erratum to RFC 4753, but some implementors did not know about it.

Implementations of RFC 4753 that included the erratum interoperate with this RFC. Those that did not may fail to interoperate, and since both use the same code point the problem could be hard to diagnose. The initiator would never receive a response and would eventually time out.

The test vectors in section 8 were also updated to show the new shared-secret format.
sections.eli5: An old rulebook said to hand over both numbers. The fix says to hand over only one. Players who missed the fix would get stuck waiting for each other.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Many of the security considerations in RFC 2409 and the IKEv2 specification apply here as well. The three groups correspond to symmetric key sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits, which lets the IKE exchange offer security comparable with the AES algorithms.

IANA updated its IKE and IKEv2 registries to list the groups, changing the reference from RFC 4753 to this document. The test vectors show the assigned group IDs: 19 for the 256-bit group, 20 for the 384-bit group and 21 for the 521-bit group. The RFC also tabulates the names these curves carry elsewhere, for example P-256, P-384 and P-521 in NIST and secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1 in SECG.
sections.eli5: The three sizes are like three strengths of lock, each as tough as a matching strength of the usual AES lock. They are listed in an official phone book under numbers 19, 20 and 21.
